# Anuruddha Saṁyutta (SN 52)

**ID:** SN 52
**Section:** Saṁyuttanikāya (sn)
**Collection:** Suttas-Early-1
**Title (Pali):** Anuruddha Saṁyutta
**Title (English, SuttaCentral):** Linked Discourses with Anuruddha
**SuttaCentral:** https://suttacentral.net/sn52

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Anuruddha Saṁyutta* (SN 52) is the fifty-second section of the *Saṁyuttanikāya*, situated within the *Mahāvagga* and comprising twenty-four discourses arranged in two chapters (*vagga*s) [SuttaCentral; Bodhi 2003; Hazra 1994]. While the Venerable Anuruddha is traditionally renowned for clairvoyance and spiritual attainments, this collection consistently presents him as an ardent exponent of mindfulness meditation (*satipaṭṭhāna*), which figures explicitly in every discourse [SuttaCentral; Gethin 2001; Bodhi 2003]. Throughout the samyutta, Anuruddha attributes his cultivation of spiritual knowledges, absorptions, and supernormal powers—such as the "power of the noble ones" (*ariya-iddhi*), the divine eye, and the destruction of the taints—to the development of the four establishments of mindfulness (e.g., SN 52.1, SN 52.15–24) [SuttaCentral; Bodhi 2003; Nyanaponika et al. 2003]. Several discourses depict Anuruddha explaining to fellow monks how *satipaṭṭhāna* enables one to endure severe bodily illness with serenity (SN 52.10), forms the habitual dwelling of both trainees and arahants (SN 52.4–5, SN 52.9), and leads steadily to the destruction of craving (SN 52.7) [Nyanaponika et al. 2003; Anālayo 2018; Wen 2011].

Scholars observe that the collection functions virtually as a supplement or appendix to the *Satipaṭṭhāna Saṁyutta* (SN 47), which itself preserves three suttas delivered by Anuruddha (SN 47.26–28) [SuttaCentral; Bodhi 2003]. Furthermore, SN 52.1 merges the internal/external and origination/vanishing extensions of the *satipaṭṭhāna* formula into a single sequence, emphasizing insight (*vipassanā*) alongside meditative calm [Bodhi 2003; Sujato 2012].

Parallels to discourses in SN 52 survive primarily in the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* (Taishō 99, rolls 19 and 27), including SĀ 537, SĀ 539, SĀ 541, and SĀ 542–543 [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. Comparative studies highlight that whereas the Pali recension underlines insight contemplations, corresponding Sarvāstivāda Āgama passages often place greater emphasis on *samādhi* or specifically single out the acquisition of the divine eye [Sujato 2012; Wen 2011]. Machine analysis by DharmaNexus identifies extensive Pali-internal text reuse across 185 texts, overwhelmingly with the *Satipaṭṭhāna Saṁyutta* (SN 47, nearly 800 shared segments), as well as the *Iddhipāda Saṁyutta* (SN 51), *Bojjhaṅga Saṁyutta* (SN 46), the *Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta* (MN 10), and the *Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅga* (Vb 7), along with cross-language alignments to the Sanskrit *Śrāvakabhūmi* and the Chinese *Saṁyuktāgama* [DharmaNexus].

**Parallels and text reuse**

- This file contains 8 suttas; 8 of them have parallels listed on SuttaCentral. Full parallels by collection: SĀ (4), Pali (1)
- Examples of full non-Pali parallels (SuttaCentral): sn52.4-5 ↔ SĀ 542-543; SN 52.6 Tatiyakaṇḍakīsutta ↔ SA 537 松林; SN 52.10 Bāḷhagilānasutta ↔ SA 541 所患; SN 52.23 Dibbacakkhusutta ↔ SA 539 松林
- Text reuse within the Pali corpus (DharmaNexus): Satipaṭṭhāna Saṁyutta (SN 47) (§2.4.1–2.7.3 ↔ §3.2.2–3.2.13); Iddhipāda Saṁyutta (SN 51) (§12.1.1_0–13.1.1_0 ↔ §14.5.16–14.5.17_0); Navakanipāta (AN 9) (§5.1.5–5.1.10 ↔ §72.3.2–72.3.7); Bojjhaṅga Saṁyutta (SN 46) (§1.3.3_2–1.4.5 ↔ §54.12.3–54.12.8_1); Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Sutta (MN 10 (PTS MN i 55)) (§2.5.2–2.7.3 ↔ §3.2–3.5); Satipaṭṭhānavibhaṅga (Vb 7) (§2.3.1–2.7.3 ↔ §1.1–2.0); Dasakanipāta (AN 10) (§3.1.2–3.1.3 ↔ §172.4.1–172.4.2); Saḷāyatana Saṁyutta (SN 35) (§8.1.3–8.3.3 ↔ §244.9.1_0–244.9.15)
- Cross-language matches (DharmaNexus): Yogācārabhūmi: Śrāvakabhūmi (SA_T06_srabhu_u) [sa]; 雜阿含經 (ZH_T02_0099) [zh]; འཕགས་པ་ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་ཁྲི་བརྒྱད་སྟོང་པ་ཞེས་བྱ་བ་ཐེག་པ་ཆེན་པོའི་མདོ། (ārya-aṣṭādaśasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā-nāma-mahāyāna-sūtra) (D0010) [bo]; Arthaviniścayasūtra (SA_K10_n260u) [sa]; ཤེས་རབ་ཀྱི་ཕ་རོལ་ཏུ་ཕྱིན་པ་སྟོང་ཕྲག་བརྒྱ་པ། (śatasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā) (D0008-3) [bo]; 雜阿含經 (ZH_T02_0099) [zh]; 增壹阿含經 (ZH_T02_0125) [zh]; BO_K05_D0010_H0012 [bo]

**Sources**

- [SuttaCentral] SuttaCentral entry for SN 52 (Anuruddhasaṁyutta) — Supplied title, discourse count, thematic summary, and curated Chinese Saṁyuktāgama parallels.
- [DharmaNexus] DharmaNexus text reuse match database for SN 52 — Identified Pali internal reuse (especially with SN 47, SN 51, MN 10, Vb 7) and cross-language alignments with Chinese and Sanskrit texts.
- [Bodhi 2003] Bhikkhu Bodhi, The Connected Discourses of the Buddha (2003) — Noted structure, role as appendix to SN 47, formulaic combinations in SN 52.1, and powers claimed through satipaṭṭhāna.
- [Gethin 2001] Rupert Gethin, The Buddhist Path to Awakening (2001) — Discussed context in the Mahāvagga and consistent association with satipaṭṭhāna in every sutta.
- [Nyanaponika et al. 2003] Nyanaponika Thera, Hellmuth Hecker, and Bhikkhu Bodhi, Great Disciples of the Buddha (2003) — Detailed specific suttas (SN 52.1, 52.2, 52.7, 52.9, 52.10, 52.15–24) and their doctrinal themes.
- [Hazra 1994] Kanai Lal Hazra, Pāli Language and Literature (1994) — Confirmed two-chapter division and core theme of Anuruddha's satipaṭṭhāna practice.
- [Anālayo 2018] Bhikkhu Anālayo, Satipaṭṭhāna Meditation: A Practice Guide (2018) — Discussed SN 52.10 regarding mindfulness used to face severe illness.
- [Wen 2011] Tzungkuen Wen, A Study of Sukkhavipassaka in Pāli Buddhism — Discussed trainee/arahant practices (SN 52.4–5, SN 52.9), bearing pain (SN 52.10), and contrast between Pali supernormal powers and Chinese divine eye.
- [Sujato 2012] Bhikkhu Sujato, A History of Mindfulness (2012) — Analyzed differences between the Pali and Sarvāstivāda Anuruddha-saṁyutta collections regarding samādhi versus vipassanā.
